title: Coordinate Reference Systems
Coordinate Reference Systems
text:
Today

Tell a geographic CRS from a projected one in R’s printout
Explain what a datum is, and when datum differences matter
Explain why every flat map distorts something, and choose a projection that protects what you measure
Use EPSG codes to name, check, and convert CRSs

title: Coordinate Reference Systems
text:
1 The failure, again

Same failure as your homework, on new data: Luxembourg
Elevation raster + 12 cantons (districts), both included with terra
Scenario: the national mapping agency sends the elevation in its own grid, EPSG:2169



Show code
library(sf)       # vector data
library(terra)    # raster data
library(dplyr)    # filter() and friends
library(spData)   # the `world` dataset, used in section 4
library(units)    # converting m^2 to km^2, used in section 4




Show code
# Elevation raster for Luxembourg
elev_file <- system.file("ex/elev.tif", package = "terra")
elev <- rast(elev_file)

# The 12 cantons of Luxembourg, as sf polygons
cantons_file <- system.file("ex/lux.shp", package = "terra")
cantons <- st_read(cantons_file)

Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 5.74414 ymin: 49.44781 xmax: 6.528252 ymax: 50.18162

Show code
# Set up the scenario: the elevation in Luxembourg's national grid.
# (project() converts a raster between CRSs; more on it in a later session.)
elev_lux <- project(elev, "EPSG:2169")
elev_lux

TipPredict



Compare the raster’s extent with the cantons’ Bounding box. If we draw the cantons on top of the elevation, what will we see?




Show code

plot(elev_lux)
plot(st_geometry(cantons), add = TRUE, border = "red")











Show code
# Loud failure: crop() checks that the layers overlap, and stops

# Silent failure: a mean elevation for each canton... all NaN
# (na.rm = TRUE is needed because elev.tif has no-data cells along the border)

The plot shows nothing: no error, no warning

5 EPSG codes: names for CRSs

One number = a complete CRS: datum + ellipsoid + projection + units
Registry maintained by IOGP: epsg.org (official), epsg.io (easier to search)
Look a code up: https://epsg.io/ + the number

TipChoose a CRS



Pick a code from the table and defend it in one sentence:

Total impervious area in each Maryland county
TRI facilities within 1 km of each Baltimore tract centroid
Asthma prevalence across the 48 contiguous states
An interactive web map for a community group









NoteSome defensible answers






5070 (equal-area) or 26985: within one state, State Plane’s area distortion is tiny. The why is the point
26985, 26918, or 32618: meters, accurate locally. Not 4326: a 1 km buffer needs meters
5070: equal-area across the country
3857 for display. Analyze in a measuring CRS, then transform for the map

title: Coordinate Reference Systems
section: 6 Back to the failure: fix it and check it
text:
6 Back to the failure: fix it and check it
Why it failed

Cantons: coordinates around 6 and 50 (degrees)
Raster: coordinates in the tens of thousands (meters)
plot() just draws numbers: cantons landed far outside the raster’s extent
crop(): no overlap → stops
extract(): no cells inside any polygon → NaN, silently

The fix

Put both layers in one CRS
Transform the vector to match the raster: moving vertices is exact, while reprojecting a raster resamples cell values



Show code
# Convert the cantons into the raster's CRS
cantons_lux <- st_transform(cantons, crs(elev_lux))

# Check 1: do the two CRSs now match?
st_crs(cantons_lux) == st_crs(elev_lux)

# Check 2: are the coordinate ranges now comparable?
st_bbox(cantons_lux)
ext(elev_lux)


[1] TRUE
     xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
 49540.31  57009.53 105922.01 138631.13 
SpatExtent : 49072.3397901184, 106196.374340225, 56455.2689687042, 139825.481555346 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)




Show code
# Check 3: look at it
plot(elev_lux)
plot(st_geometry(cantons_lux), add = TRUE, border = "red")











Show code
# The zonal mean now works: one number per canton
good <- extract(elev_lux, cantons_lux, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
cantons_lux$elev_mean <- good$elevation

# Check 4: no missing values, and plausible elevations (meters)
sum(is.na(cantons_lux$elev_mean))
summary(cantons_lux$elev_mean)


[1] 0
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  239.6   312.9   322.3   339.7   374.2   467.1 








WarningLabeling is not converting




st_transform() converts: the numbers change
st_set_crs() / st_crs(x) <- ... only relabels: the numbers stay
Relabel only when a file has no CRS and you know what it should be
AI assistants sometimes suggest relabeling as a “fix” for a mismatch:



Show code
# Wrong: claims the degrees are now meters
cantons_relabeled <- st_set_crs(cantons, 2169)


Warning: st_crs<- : replacing crs does not reproject data; use st_transform for that


Show code
st_bbox(cantons_relabeled)


     xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
 5.744140 49.447807  6.528252 50.181622 



R warns, and the bbox gives it away: still 5.7 to 50.2
In EPSG:2169, numbers that small sit at the grid’s origin: in France, about 120 km southwest of Luxembourg’s center

text:
7 In your code








Question
Function
What to look for




What CRS is this?
Print the object; st_crs(x); crs(r, describe = TRUE)
Name, EPSG code, units


Degrees or meters?
st_is_longlat(x); is.lonlat(r)
TRUE means degrees


Do my layers match?
st_crs(a) == st_crs(b); compare st_bbox() and ext()
Same CRS; ranges that overlap


Does it look right?
plot() the raster, then the vector with add = TRUE
Lines where you expect them


Convert a vector
st_transform(x, crs)
The bbox numbers change


Convert a raster
project(r, crs)
Resamples values (later session)


Label a CRS-less file
st_set_crs(x, crs)
Only when the CRS is missing and known




Check the CRS before combining two layers; check the result after
Most CRS mistakes don’t produce errors. They produce wrong answers

title: Coordinate Reference Systems
text:
8 Check yourself






Note1. A bounding box reads xmin: 316268 ymin: 4295630 xmax: 334407 ymax: 4318264. Degrees or meters? Projected or geographic?






Meters, so projected: longitudes stop at ±180, latitudes at ±90
Hundreds of thousands and millions look like UTM (this is Washington, DC, in UTM zone 18N)










Note2. extract(r, polygons, fun = mean) gives you some NaNs. Name three possible causes, and how you’d tell them apart.






All NaN: the layers don’t overlap. Usually a CRS mismatch (today’s failure); sometimes the raster covers a different area. Compare st_bbox() and ext()
Some NaN, with na.rm = TRUE: those polygons fall only on no-data cells or outside the raster’s edge. Plot the polygons on the raster and look at where the NaN ones are
Many NaN, without na.rm = TRUE: any polygon that touches even one no-data cell returns NaN. Here, 9 of 12 cantons did. Add na.rm = TRUE, and decide whether a partial average is acceptable










Note3. An AI suggests st_transform(tri, 2263) before buffering TRI facilities in Baltimore by 1,000. Look up EPSG:2263. What’s wrong?






It’s NAD83 / New York Long Island (ftUS): the wrong place, and the units are US feet
A buffer of 1,000 would be 1,000 ft (about 305 m), not 1 km
Baltimore is outside its area of use, so distortion is larger too
Better: 26985 (Maryland, meters) or 26918 / 32618 (UTM 18N)










Note4. TRI facilities are in EPSG:4326 and tracts in EPSG:4269, about a meter apart. What happens if you st_join() them without transforming? Loud or silent?






Loud: st_join() stops with st_crs(x) == st_crs(y) is not TRUE
sf requires identical CRSs and can’t judge whether a meter matters for your question
Fix: transform one to match the other (or both to a projected CRS you’ll measure in)
Compare with extract() in section 1, which failed silently
